title: Since When Were We Resting?
mood: The power comes back to the street all at once, and nobody has time to rest.

hero.alt: Under a sky streaked with red fire, Guinevere kneels in a ruined street as her two round cat-eared drones float up beside her, and above the towers a huge dark ship burns.

segs.t: Guinevere was on one knee in the gap.
The last Ender off the heap lay across her boots, its core cracked. Her fist had done that. Then her side had given out, and the stones had come up to meet her knee.
Her knuckles bled into the rain. Vexana stood over her, the dark staff raised. Another Ender was already climbing the heap.
Then the hum stopped.
It had sat in her teeth since her wings went out. She had stopped hearing it. Now it was gone, and the quiet rang.
The magenta went out of the air. The rain was only gray again.
Out on the bay road the hanging slabs came down all at once, and the street jumped under her knee.
Down at the mouth of the cut, smoke drifted over the stones where she had fallen. Two small yellow lights rose out of it.
Nothing else had lit yet. They were first.
She knew their whine. All this time it had been missing from the street.
Her drones came up the cut side by side, ears up. At the heap the right drone swerved and cracked the climbing Ender across the head, and it went back down the far side. Showing off, as usual.
Guinevere held out her bleeding hand. They came to it and hung there, one on each side, humming.
Fists first,
she thought.
Then the drones.
Every night in the training hall it had been that order. Today too.
She laughed. It hurt her side, and she laughed anyway.
“And where have you two been?” she asked them.
The right one bumped her cheek.
She sat back on the stones with both drones beside her and looked up.
Over the Academy the Storm Citadel hung in a sky streaked red. Fire ran along its black ribs. The whole ship was tilting. Burning pieces broke off it and blew away toward the bay.
Minutes ago, between one Ender and the next, she had seen lightning go up from the Academy’s roofs into that ship. It was white, like the lightning that had come down into this street.
At her collar something went warm.
She looked down. The gold star was lit.
Vexana was looking at her own wrist. Through the cloth of her right sleeve a second star shone.
For a long moment Vexana did not move. Then violet wings opened at her back and lifted her off the stones.
Down on the bay road, past the mouth of the cut, three giants stood dark where they had stopped.
Vexana lifted her free hand to them. One by one their yellow eyes lit. They straightened. The last one bent and took its sword up off the stones.
Vexana called down to them.
“The crown of the sun will never be extinguished!”
Three swords came up together.
Layla lay on the stones in the gap, where she had dropped. The dead Ender’s claw lay beside her hand. Fanny stood over her, facing the heap.
Two yellow lights came up the cut over her head. Guinevere’s drones.
Then the strap across her back began to hum. Her cannon was waking. She did not need to look. The cells along its stock were lighting cyan, from the bottom up, every one.
The rig at Fanny’s hips coughed and caught. Light ran down both her blades, and arcs jumped off their edges.
Fanny lifted them and looked at the light.
“A strong Aspirant spirit becomes the blade that cuts through despair.”
She said it low, to the blades.

Layla looked up the street behind the wall. At the top of the cut two Enders lay dead on the stones among the wounded. Ruby knelt beside Angela with one hand on her shoulder. Angela’s arm still sparked at the elbow.
Pink light opened over them. It curved down around the wounded on every side.
Angela’s voice came on the channel, bright.
“Battery recharged!”
On the channel behind it, Ruby laughed once.
Down the street the Enders were still coming. One was already on the heap.
Fanny looked down at Layla and held out a hand.
“All rested up?”
Her face was perfectly straight.
Layla took the hand. “Since when were we resting?”
Fanny’s straight face broke as she pulled her to her feet. They climbed onto the heap and stood back to back over the street, the cannon and the blades lit.

media.alt: Official art: Fanny, short orange hair and a red scarf, and Layla, long pink twin tails, charge forward side by side, Fanny's blades and Layla's great cannon raised.

segs.t: The command deck.
Rain still came in through the empty frame. Mr. Bunny hung at Chang’e’s shoulder, one ear crooked.
The hum went out of the floor.
On her screen every flat line jumped at once. The first one she saw was gold, in the bay road cut.
Around her chair the crescents flickered on the floor. They lifted one by one, white edged with pink, and began to turn around her again.
“Good morning,” she told them.
At the broken window Lesley stood watching the district below. Down the hill, gold and cyan were coming back in the streets.
“There’s still... hope... ah.”
Under Lesley’s hand the coil on the rifle had woken. Chang’e heard it come up to its note. She had tuned that note herself.
Lesley was looking down at it.
Chang’e read the sky the way she read a console.
Above the window the Storm Citadel hung over the Academy. It listed as it burned. The long thing in the middle of it read nothing now. The field was dead at its source.
She had called it a spine.
Somebody cut it,
she thought.
Lesley looked out at the bell tower, small under the burning ship. Its roof was empty.
Over the bay the Singularity’s mouth still hung open. Behind its light, faint, sat the Matrix’s signature.
“It isn’t dead,” said Chang’e. “It’s only gone back.”
“For now,” said Lesley.
At the bottom of the screen the thin trace from the morning still ran. It still had no name. Beside it the light for mobile support still blinked.
Chang’e did not look up from the console. She touched Mr. Bunny’s crooked ear. “You owe me a pudding.”
Since the founding, a cup had turned up outside the lab door after every long night. Caramel, the spoon laid square across the lid, never a note. Neither of them had ever said a word about it.
“Two,” said Lesley.
She came back from the window and stood behind the chair. Her hand rested on its back. Chang’e left it there.
The bay road cut.
They fought on at the mouth of the cut.
Vexana’s giants held the bay road. Guinevere’s drones took whatever came high. From the heap behind them Fanny’s arcs went out across the road, and Layla’s cannon fired on her own count.
The Enders kept coming up out of the water.
Between one rush and the next, Guinevere went down on one knee again, a hand on her side. She was looking up. Vexana came down beside her and looked where she looked.
Up in the burning hull, through the holes in its side, two lights met. They broke apart, and met again.
“Is she winning?” asked Guinevere.
“I don’t know,” said Vexana.
The lights came out through the hull, one after the other. For a moment the smoke hid them. Then they were far out over the bay, climbing into open sky, and the cloud closed behind them.

The Citadel’s storm was thinning to rags. Without it the ship sank. All day the wind had blown toward the Singularity’s mouth. Now it took the ship and carried it back out over the bay, low and burning.
Vexana had walked its hanging streets once.
It drifted into the mouth, and the black point at the center took it. The wreck broke apart and blew up inside. Light tore across the portal from rim to rim, and flickered.
Nothing of it came down on the city.
Vexana watched the light run along the rim. “It’s torn,” she said. “It isn’t closed.”
Guinevere was looking at the empty sky where the lights had gone. “Where’s Selena?”
Nobody answered.
On the bay road the Enders were still coming.
Guinevere got up. Her drones came to her shoulders, and gold wings opened at her back.
She said it without looking round. “Same place. Next year.”
Vexana had not planned on a next year. On her desk, under two felt dolls, a card still said it in her own small square letters.
“Same place,” she said.
They went up off the stones together, gold beside violet, both stars lit, into the Enders still coming.
